d.g: Like a dwarf; being especially small or stunted.
d.x: […] now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him, like a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief.

d.g: Of, pertaining to, or made by or for dwarves.
d.x: Dwarfish axes are some of the finest weapons available.

dwarfish.e: English dwarf Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-isk Old English -isċ Middle English -ish English -ish English dwarfish From dwarf + -ish.

d.g: present participle and gerund of dwindle
declining; growing less
d.x: There is dwindling support for New Labour.

d.g: A gradual reduction to nothing.

Any member of a race of beings from (especially Scandinavian and other Germanic) folklore, usually depicted as having some sort of supernatural powers and being skilled in crafting and metalworking, often as short with long beards, and sometimes as clashing with elves.
d.x: [T]he elf king and his queen made a royal progress every noon with a splendid retinue of dwarves and sprites, […]

d.g: A person of short stature, often one whose limbs are disproportionately small in relation to the body as compared with typical adults, usually as the result of a genetic condition.
An animal, plant or other thing much smaller than the usual of its sort.
A dwarf star.

dwarf.e: From Middle English dwergh, dwerw, dwerf, from Old English dweorg, from Proto-West Germanic *dwerg, from Proto-Germanic *dwergaz. …

d.g: The quality of being dwarfish.
The condition of being a dwarf (person of short stature).
d.x: Studies of disproportionate dwarfisms in animals have revealed the importance of core proteins an sulfation in the development of cartilage.

d.g: The quality of being puny or inferior.
d.x: Childish, childish to the core: that's why they're so good at nursing, they're arrested in a state of permanent intellectual dwarfism themselves!

dwarfism.e: English dwarf Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English dwarfism From dwarf + -ism.

d.g: A boring, studious, or socially inept person.
d.x: I may be dumb, but I'm not a dweeb.

dweeb.e: From 1968 US college slang, probably related to feeb. The 1980s backronym Dim-Witted Eastern-Educated Boor derives from apparent social and attitudinal differences between West Coast and East Coast US, and describes a stereotypical Ivy League graduate from Harvard, Yale, etc. Etymology tree ▲ English feebinflu. …

d.g: An inhabitant of a specific place; an inhabitant or denizen.
d.x: The new couple are apartment dwellers.

d.g: A house or place in which a person lives; a habitation, a home.
d.x: The old house served as a dwelling for Albert.

d.g: present participle and gerund of dwell

dwelling.e: From Middle English dwellynge, dwellyng (“delay, continuance, abode”), equivalent to dwell + -ing. More at dwell.

d.g: A period of time in which a system or component remains in a given state.
A brief pause in the motion of part of a mechanism to allow an operation to be completed.
A planned delay in a timed control program.

In a petrol engine, the period of time the ignition points are closed to let current flow through the ignition coil in between each spark. This is measured as an angle in degrees around the camshaft in the distributor which controls the points, for example in a 4-cylinder engine it might be 55° (spark at 90° intervals, points closed for 55° between each).

d.g: To decrease, shrink, diminish, reduce in size or intensity.
d.x: Their supplies began to dwindle after a week.

d.g: To fall away in quality; degenerate, sink.
d.x: VVearie Seu'nights, nine times nine, / Shall he dvvindle, peake, and pine: […]

d.g: To lessen; to bring low.
d.x: Our drooping days are dwindled down to nought.

d.g: To break up or disperse.
d.x: there were only five hundred foot and three hundred horse left with him, for the blocking of Plymouth; the rest were dwindled away

dwindle.e: Frequentative form of dwine, from Middle English dwynen, from Old English dwīnan (“to waste away”), from Proto-West Germanic *dwīnan, from Proto-Germanic *dwīnaną. It is equivalent to dwine + -le, akin to Old Norse dvena, dvína, Dutch verdwijnen (“to disappear, dwindle”).
